rss_0_1790805685.title: Trump administration diverts human rights funds to push far-right agenda abroad
rss_0_1790805685.text:
With hours left before the funding expires, the Trump administration is pushing to direct more than $175m of the state department’s flagship human rights fund to a slate of awards that includes a huge $40m grant for an anti-communism fund, support for a group advancing white Afrikaner rights in South Africa, a campaign against Brazil’s supreme court and programs that would reward ideological allies in Europe who protect “western civilizational norms”.

On Wednesday, the state department obligated the funds to the grantees hours before the deadline despite congressional concerns and requests not to do so, according to a source familiar with the negotiations. The state department declined to comment on questions from the Guardian specifically on whether it had obligated the funds and had “blown” holds from Congress due to concerns about the money’s use.

Critics have focused on 43 awards of a combined $176.9m that will bolster rightwing and conservative causes around the world while probably angering US allies over interference in internal politics. The Guardian has seen a sample of the controversial grants, which make up most of the $205m in funding that Congress has appropriated for the entire Human Rights and Democracy Fund (HRDF).

Sources with knowledge of the grant process have told the Guardian that the awards were personally lobbied for by members of the Trump administration, and reflect interests that include JD Vance’s warnings of the collapse of traditional western values in Europe and Stephen Miller’s push against immigration and to support white minorities in countries like South Africa.

“The story for me is the high-level – including White House-directed – attention on these programs,” said a person familiar with the discussions over the democracy awards. “These awards have been briefed at the highest levels of the department and have buy-in from the White House.”

The proposed awards represent a significant shift in US support for dissidents, human rights defenders and civil society groups under authoritarian governments. The new slate includes projects in wealthy nations, and those focused on opposition to regulation, Brexit, migration, anti-communism, Christian protection and opposition to “gender ideology”, offering a window into how the Trump administration is redefining what qualifies as human rights and merits tens of millions of dollars in US foreign assistance.

“Congress appropriated money for the democracy fund on a bipartisan basis to support defenders of human rights, to assist victims of human rights violations and to instead promote the growth of democracy abroad,” said Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the US Senate committee on foreign relations.

“The Trump administration’s proposals would use taxpayer funds to promote far-right organizations and programs in established democracies. This is a waste of resources and undermines United States values and relations with democratic partners, including allies in Europe.”

The largest award, of $40m, was directed to a consortium led by the Victims of Communism Memorial Foundation (VOC), an anti-communist non-profit that has received far smaller grants in the past. A state department vetting document seen by the Guardian records $96,997 in previous contracts in the last five years between the foundation and the department, all in the 2022 fiscal year, and notes that it had been vetted in 2019 in connection with tickets to the foundation’s gala. The vetting document also identifies Andrew Bremberg, a former Trump White House domestic policy adviser and US ambassador to the UN European office, as a “senior leader” of the foundation.

In July, ProPublica reported that Samuel Samson, a 27-year-old deputy assistant secretary overseeing the new grants, was linked to senior members of VOC through his studies at the Christian conservative Hillsdale College graduate program. (A state department official then told the outlet that the relationship had nothing to do with the grant).

Samson has described the US and Europe as partners in a shared civilizational struggle. Samson toured Austria, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia last December – all countries that were floated to receive a $2m grant to counter migration weaponized by Russia and Belarus – and criticized NGOs that previous administrations had worked with for promoting what he called radical concepts, including gender theory and DEI.

The state department did not comment on individual grants but said the programs were still in “active deliberation”, that awardees would meet guidelines for federal grants, and that all programming would undergo a “standard and rigorous vetting process by grant professionals”.

“Our programming in Europe aims to support our European allies in defending those rights and principles, along with their civilizational self-confidence and sovereignty from those who seek to undermine them,” a state department official said. “The national security strategy highlights our priorities in Europe which includes advancing political liberty, promoting free speech, and collaborating with European partners to jointly support European revitalization and civilizational self-confidence.”

Under the legislation authorizing the fund, the money must be assigned by 30 September, the end of the fiscal year, when unobligated funds typically lapse. Shaheen, the ranking member of the Senate foreign relations committee, has put a partial “hold” on giving the grants to some of the controversial awardees – setting up a showdown with the state department with just hours left for the money to be obligated.

The Guardian first reported that Trump officials had drawn up no-bid grants aimed at rightwing and anti-immigration causes in Europe. ProPublica similarly reported that there were at least a dozen no-bid grants earmarked for rightwing projects.

The document now shows how much of the fund the plan takes up, and which awards have since been dropped.

A $1m award titled “Countering Lawfare and Censorship in Brazil” would fund civil society groups opposing what it calls judicial overreach and censorship by Brazil’s supreme court. The Trump administration sanctioned the Brazilian justice Alexandre de Moraes last year after lobbying by Eduardo Bolsonaro, son of the former president.

A program titled “Promoting Western Civilization Allies” would be limited to implementers who do not subscribe to “ideologically weaponized accounts of human rights, such as gender ideology”, according to the document, and will receive $2m. It names possible recipients in Poland, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary, and the Balkans with “anti-communist” and “natural rights” approaches.

One award was allocated to document “democratic backsliding” in Europe tied to “mass and illegal migration” and legislation by “supra-national entities”, while a $1m journalism consortium would push back against designations of “trusted” media outlets. The list also includes $2m for early-warning networks protecting Christians in Nigeria.

And a $3m no-bid award would go to the Jobs Foundation, a UK group run by Matthew Elliott, who led the Vote Leave campaign. The grant, titled “Countering Overregulation to Advance American Investment”, would promote a “common good capitalism index” and pro-business policy, including how the foundation promoted Brexit as a chance to cut the UK’s climate regulations.

The document also shows that a proposed $5m no-bid grant to the Free Speech Union, the British group founded by Toby Young, has been marked “withdrawn”. When the award was first reported in July, Young said the group had never applied for or received US government money (though Trump officials had reportedly met with the group during a European tour late last year).

The grant would have paid the group to campaign against online safety and hate speech laws, including Britain’s Online Safety Act, a law passed under the Conservatives in 2023. Meant to protect children from harmful content and is enforced by Ofcom, its age-verification rules – which took effect last year – have drawn constant criticism from the Trump administration, which cast them as censorship.

The Free Speech Union is the second British group to drop off the list. A $7m no-bid award to 878, a thinktank whose stated missions include restoring Judeo-Christian culture and “ending mass migration and deporting illegal immigrants”, was abandoned in July after pushback from Congress. It was founded by Jacob Rees-Mogg, who served as Brexit opportunities minister and business secretary before losing his seat at the 2024 election, and now presents on GB News.

The British awards would have sent $15m in US taxpayer money to groups run by two sitting Conservative peers and a former cabinet minister, regarding issues including online safety law to migration.

rss_1_1790805685.title: South African leader urges men to speak up on gender-based violence after series of killings
rss_1_1790805685.text:
South Africa’s president has called on men to take more responsibility for violence against women as he announced measures to tackle the problem, amid anger at authorities over a recent wave of murders.

Cyril Ramaphosa acknowledged that not enough had been done to protect women. He said police would be reviewing unsolved murders, attempted murders and serious sexual offences against women and children, as well as producing a funded plan to reduce the forensic backlog for such cases, both within 60 days.

In a televised speech on Tuesday night, the president said local governments would have five months to address issues that compromised women’s safety, from broken streetlights to overgrown public spaces and abandoned buildings. He added that he had tasked five ministers to come up with a plan within 60 days to reduce alcohol-fuelled violence.

View image in fullscreen Cyril Ramaphosa acknowledged that not enough had been done to protect women. Photograph: Jairus Mmutle/South African Communications and Information Services/AP

“Alcohol does not cause gender-based violence and it can never excuse it. Responsibility always lies with the perpetrator,” Ramaphosa said. “But harmful alcohol use is a significant aggravating factor in interpersonal violence and it must be addressed as part of our wider prevention effort.

“Women should not have to live in fear because government has failed to repair a light, clear a public space, process evidence or enforce a law.”

South Africa has been gripped by grief and fury after the discovery of 11 women’s bodies dumped across Ekurhuleni, the municipality adjoining Johannesburg to the east, since 15 July. Eight of the women were found in the last three weeks, including Elizabeth “Tsontso” Moselakgomo, who was discovered on 12 September after she went missing when she went for a run after work.

View image in fullscreen People take part in a memorial run in honour of Elizabeth ‘Tsontso’ Moselakgomo. Photograph: Alet Pretorius/Reuters

Ramaphosa said suspects had been arrested in connection with three of the killings and that the other cases would not be left to go cold. He added that police had not found evidence that a serial killer was responsible for all 11 killings, but that all possibilities were still being investigated.

He directly addressed South African men, urging them to challenge relatives, friends and colleagues who harassed, humiliated or abused women. “It is time for good men to stop being silent men,” he said.

“For too long, gender-based violence has been treated as a woman’s problem to solve. Women march, the women of our country organise, they speak out, they protest, they confront and they comfort survivors,” Ramaphosa said.

“Women change their routes home. Avoid going out at night and warn one another about dangerous places and dangerous men. We have placed the burden of male violence on women. That must change.”

View image in fullscreen Students gather at the University of Cape Town during a vigil for victims of gender-based violence and femicide, while calling for stronger action against violence against women. Photograph: Esa Alexander/Reuters

Activists expressed their frustration that solid policy actions had not been taken years ago and scepticism that the measures Ramaphosa had announced would work.

Shenilla Mohamed, the executive director of Amnesty International South Africa, said: “These are not new issues and as a country we have been talking about ways to tackle the high numbers of [gender-based violence and femicide], especially since 2019 when women took to the streets to protest, and yet here we are again in the face of continued attacks against women.

“Amnesty International South Africa also notes the timelines put in place by the president, but this will only mean something if it results in action, and if there are consequences for inaction.”

Mpiwa Mangwiro-Tsanga and Bafana Khumalo, of Sonke Gender Justice, an NGO, said: “Our concern … is that the response remains heavily weighted towards what happens after violence has already occurred.”

They added: “Investigating unresolved cases, processing forensic evidence and repairing unsafe public spaces are necessary, but they do not constitute a comprehensive prevention strategy. It is concerning that the president is asking municipalities to do what is actually their mandate and yet they do not deliver on these.”

rss_2_1790805686.title: Burundi agrees to receive ‘third-country’ migrant deportees from US
rss_2_1790805686.text:
Burundi has agreed to join a clutch of ⁠other African nations in receiving migrants from other countries deported from the US under ⁠Donald Trump’s hardline ⁠immigration ​policy.

However, Burundi will only accept those not accused of crime or terrorism links, said ⁠Nancy Ninette Mutoni, a spokesperson for the country’s president, Évariste Ndayishimiye. Tuesday’s announcement gave no details of numbers, timing or financial ⁠details.

Washington has sent so-called “third-country deportees” to about half ​a dozen African nations ‌as well as many other countries, often where they have no ties, have never been and find themselves detained indefinitely, under opaque deals ‌that Senate Democrats say have cost tens of millions of ‌dollars.

In many cases, deportees had secured legal protections from immigration courts in the US against repatriation. But rights groups say the third-country deals allow the US to circumvent those protections.

Mutoni said preparations were under way to arrange accommodation, ‌living conditions and integration into local communities in Burundi. “Receiving them requires serious planning – where they will stay, what they ​will eat and how they will live alongside the local population,” she said.

“If they choose to join Burundian citizens and make a valuable contribution to national development, the law ⁠will be respected,” she said, regarding potential citizenship.

Burundi aimed ​to both ​strengthen diplomatic relations and provide ​hospitality to people in need, the spokesperson ​added.

The US ‌state department ​did not ​immediately respond to requests for comment while a spokesperson for the Burundi foreign ministry said details of the agreement were not yet available.

rss_3_1790805686.title: DRC politician beaten to death after radio appearance about Ebola outbreak
rss_3_1790805686.text:
A senior member of the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s ruling party was beaten to death on Sunday after appearing on a radio programme to raise awareness about the Ebola outbreak, a party representative has said.

Marie-Celestin Karondwa, the acting president of the Union for Democracy and Social Progress (UDPS) party’s federal executive committee in Butembo, a new hotspot for the outbreak, was attacked after taking part in a ​radio show during which he ‌promoted prevention measures for the disease, ‌the UDPS federation in the city said in a statement, Reuters reported.

The party ‌said the attackers beat Karondwa, stole his belongings and set his house on fire, and that he later died from his injuries.

It was not immediately clear who carried out the attack, how many people were involved or what motivated it, but the party said Karondwa was “an innocent victim for having defended ‌the party’s position on the existence of the Ebola virus disease … and the threat it poses to ​the population”.

Karondwa’s death comes after a series of attacks on healthcare workers and treatment centres that experts say are fuelled by rumours and misinformation about the disease and distrust of health responders.

The incidents have included violence, riots and property damage and the disruption of essential services. On Saturday, ​armed men attacked a hand-washing ​checkpoint in the nearby Beni territory, killing at least one ​person and wounding ‌several others, a ​local civil ​society group reported.

First identified in 1976 in what is now the DRC, Ebola is a highly contagious and often fatal viral disease that affects humans and non-human primates. It spreads through body fluids or contaminated materials and causes organ damage, blood vessel impairment and sometimes severe internal and external bleeding.

The current outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no approved treatment or vaccine. It was first announced on 15 May and has infected 8,067 people and killed 3,901, according to data from the DRC’s health ministry.

Cases of the disease have been confirmed in seven provinces.

The outbreak is the largest and deadliest in the DRC’s history and second only ​globally to ​the 2014-16 outbreak in west Africa, which infected ​more than ‌28,600 people ​and ​killed more than 11,000.

Data from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention shows the current outbreak has outpaced the west African one.

Last month, the World Health Organization warned it was on track to surpass the west Africa outbreak. Experts say the spread of the disease has been intensified by several factors, including conflict, aid cuts and the attacks on healthcare workers and treatment centres.

Reuters contributed to this report

rss_4_1790805687.title: At least 27 dead after two mass shootings in South Africa, police say
rss_4_1790805687.text:
Two separate mass shootings near South Africa’s two biggest cities killed at least 27 people, as the country grapples with one of the world’s highest murder rates amid investigations into corruption and criminality within the police.

The South African police service said on Sunday that 17 people were killed on Saturday night when eight suspects armed with AK-47 assault rifles and pistols opened fire at a bar in Wedela township, about 50 miles south-west of central Johannesburg. At least 15 other people sustained gunshot injuries in that attack, police said.

In a separate statement, police said 10 people had been killed in a mass shooting at an entertainment venue selling grilled meat, known as shisanyama, in Lwandle, near Cape Town. Another 11 people were wounded in that shooting. Police said they were searching for multiple suspects, without giving an exact number.

The two attacks happened days after a mass shooting by three gunmen at a house party near the east-coast city of Durban killed 11 people, including a pregnant woman.

No arrests had been made in the two latest mass shootings, police said.

South Africa has struggled with high rates of violent crime for years, but the series of mass shootings this week were shocking even to a country used to some of the highest violent crime rates in the world.

“This ​cannot go on like this,” South Africa’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, told local TV news channels. “This is the level of criminality that we must bring down, and our security forces are now going ⁠to continue pulling out all stops.”

View image in fullscreen A man clears the debris in a shisanyama in Lwandle after gunmen stormed the premises. Photograph: Gianluigi Guercia/AFP/Getty Images

Police in the province of Gauteng said on Sunday morning they had launched a manhunt for the unidentified eight suspects in the Johannesburg tavern shooting, with no arrests yet made.

“It is alleged that patrons were drinking inside and outside the tavern when the suspects arrived and opened fire on those outside,” a police spokesperson, Capt Tintswalo Sibeko, said in a statement.

“The suspects then entered the tavern and continued shooting at patrons inside. The suspects were reportedly armed with AK-47 rifles and pistols. They allegedly searched some patrons and took their cellphones before fleeing the scene in two unidentified motor vehicles. Two vehicles were also set alight during the incident.”

While many local residents did not want to speak about the shooting, one said that illegal goldminers were active in the area. Gauteng province’s police commissioner, Tommy Mthombeni, told reporters that one of their lines of inquiry was that the shooting was part of a “turf war in terms of illegal mining”.

Illegal miners, known as zama zamas, which means “to take a chance” in Zulu, are usually part of powerful gangs, with multiple mass shooting incidents around Johannesburg blamed on them in recent years.

Mthombeni also said Saturday’s shooting could have been retaliation for another at the same tavern about a month ago.

View image in fullscreen Members of South Africa’s forensic pathology service and armed forces personnel inspect the scene of the shooting at the bar in Wedela. Photograph: Emmanuel Croset/AFP/Getty Images

Western Cape police said they had set up a team led by serious violent crime detectives to investigate the Cape Town shooting, in which the gunmen entered the shinsanyama venue at about 1.46am on Sunday and starting shooting at customers.

“Five individuals died on the scene while five others succumbed to injuries sustained after being transported to medical facilities,” the statement said. “Eleven others are receiving medical treatment for injuries sustained … Detectives are hard at work in search of the perpetrators of the shooting incident, with no arrests effected yet. The identities of the deceased persons will be released once their next of kin are informed.”

A police official said that “business jealousy might have been the issue”, citing reports that people had been buying cheaper alcohol elsewhere and then bringing it to the venue to drink.

South Africans are already reeling after the discovery of numerous women’s bodies near Johannesburg’s airport since July, most of which were found in the last few weeks. The killings led to renewed anger about high rates of gender-based violence in the country, and have piled pressure on police and politicians to do more about it.

Alongside this, the Madlanga commission judicial inquiry has been examining allegations of corruption and criminality within the police in televised hearings for the past year.

South Africa had a murder rate of almost 40 per 100,000 people in 2024, according to the UN office on drugs and crime. That was the ninth-highest in the world that year, with only Caribbean countries higher.

In the 12 months to 30 June, more than 22,700 people were murdered in South Africa, according to police data.

Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report

rss_5_1790805687.title: Mighty Sparrow, the Trinidad and Tobago singer known as the ‘calypso king of the world’, dies aged 91
rss_5_1790805687.text:
Slinger Francisco, known on stage as the Mighty Sparrow and dubbed the “calypso king of the world”, has died aged 91.

Francisco, who got his breakthrough in calypso music with his 1956 hit song Jean and Dinah, died peacefully surrounded by his family in New York on Sunday, his family said in a statement.

His death came after a “brief illness,” the statement said without disclosing any other details.

“He was an institution in the entertainment industry, well admired for his skill and finesse as a singer, songwriter and mentor; beloved by many,” Francisco’s family said.

View image in fullscreen Mighty Sparrow performs at the Melkweg in 1989 in Amsterdam, the Netherlands. Photograph: Frans Schellekens/Redferns

The Mighty Sparrow will be remembered as “a defining voice of our culture, a master storyteller and a towering figure whose music helped carry calypso from Trinidad and Tobago to the world,” the Trinbago Unified Calypsonians’ Organisation said in a statement.

Born in the coastal town of Grand Roy, Grenada, in July 1935, Francisco was just a toddler when he migrated with his parents to Trinidad and Tobago in 1937.

Trinidad and Tobago is the birthplace of calypso music, and was where the name and persona of the Mighty Sparrow emerged to produce a list of hit songs in the genre: Both of Them, Congo Man, Mr. Walker, The Lizard and many more.

Birdie, as Francisco was also affectionately known, recorded hundreds of songs in a career that spanned six decades. He performed in several countries around the world, including at famous venues such as New York City’s Madison Square Garden.

Throughout his career, Francisco’s goal was to advance the calypso art form, according to Dr Rudolph Ottley, a Trinidadian cultural historian and author.

“The Mighty Sparrow was the supreme entertainer, a cultural revolutionary and one of the world’s greatest Calypsonians,” Ottley told the Associated Press.

Trinidad and Tobago has honored the composer and performer with national awards, and in 1987 the University of the West Indies conferred an honorary doctor of letters on Francisco.

rss_6_1790805687.title: Hurricane Nolo still threatens Hawaii as Mexico’s Baja braces for Hurricane Polo
rss_6_1790805687.text:
Hurricane Nolo was moving away from the Hawaiian islands on Sunday, but the threat of heavy rain, flash flooding and strong winds persisted in areas of the island chain still recovering from previous storms.

Nolo was about 365 miles (585km) south-south-west of Honolulu and moving away from the Big Island at about 12mph (19km/h). But the Hawaii county civil defense agency said a high wind warning, wind advisory and high surf advisory remained in effect for parts of the island through Sunday evening as Nolo’s maximum sustained winds rose to 115mph.

Nolo was expected to strengthen further and turn toward the north-west by Sunday night, though the US National Hurricane Center said the storm’s center would remain well south and south-west of the Hawaiian Islands. The storm was expected to approach the Papahānaumokuākea marine national monument, a national conservation area, early this week.

Forecasters said Nolo’s outer bands could cause life-threatening flooding and mudslides, with parts of the Big Island possibly getting up to 20in (50cm ) of rain. Heavy rain also was expected on the other islands.

“Don’t venture out if you don’t have to into the dangerous flooding environment, but also high winds. We can have trees and power lines down,” said Michael Brennan, director of the National Hurricane Center.

Heavy rain fell across the southern part of the Big Island on Saturday afternoon, prompting partial closures of one of the main highways linking Kailua-Kona in the west to Hilo in the east.

View image in fullscreen Members of the Hawaii army national guard help a resident leave his home as rainwater from nearby Hurricane Nolo floods a section of Mamalahoa highway on Saturday. Photograph: Gregory Bull/AP

Near Naalehu, at the island’s southern point, national guard members were seen guiding a man driving through flooded streets as he tried to leave his home during a downpour. More than 120 guard members were activated on the island, part of roughly 400 statewide after the governor issued an emergency proclamation.

Residents are still recovering from Hurricane Lala , which produced heavy rain and winds strong enough to sweep about 100 homes off their foundations on the Big Island.

About a dozen people were in the water on Saturday morning at Carlsmith Beach Park in Hilo on the Big Island, despite signs saying the strand was closed. Andrea Gill was out for her regular swim before heading back home to hunker down with family.

Shop owners boarded up businesses, and events were canceled. Gill said storms were common, but hurricanes were rare. She was holding out hope that the islands might not get the full impact.

“We’re used to lots of rain. We’re not used to wind. So it’s always a blessing when we don’t get the wind from the hurricane,” Gill said.

Donald Trump recently approved an emergency declaration, authorizing the Federal Emergency Management Agency (Fema) to coordinate assistance and provide funding support.

Hawaiian Electric, the state’s primary utility, said crews helping restore power in Kauai after this month’s Hurricane Lowell returned to Oahu, Maui and the Big Island in response to Nolo.

The Pacific has been unusually active this season, according to the National Weather Service lead forecaster Bob Oravec, with storm activity running above average during what is already the peak of hurricane season. He said that pattern is consistent with El Niño years, when the Pacific often sees more tropical storms and hurricanes.

View image in fullscreen Yellow tapes on Medano Beach on Sunday as Hurricane Polo approaches Baja California Sur, in Cabo San Lucas, Mexico. Photograph: Raquel Cunha/Reuters

Meanwhile, parts of Mexico’s Baja California peninsula awaited the arrival of another major hurricane with a similar name, Polo, as it edged closer after lashing other parts of the country’s south-west coast with rain and strong winds.

Hurricane Polo remained a dangerous category 3 hurricane with top sustained winds of 125mph and was moving to the north-north-west at 12mph about 275 miles (445km) south-south-west of Cabo San Lucas at the peninsula’s southern tip, US hurricane forecasters said on Sunday afternoon. It was moving to the north at 12mph.

Mexico’s National Meteorological Service, or SMN, said in a post on the social media platform X that Polo was expected to make a Baja landfall on Monday.

Mexico’s government issued a hurricane warning along the coast of mainland Mexico from Huatabampito to Guaymas.

The Mexican navy said in a statement that it had gathered personnel and humanitarian aid in the ports of Guaymas and Mazatlán, on Mexico’s Pacific coast, and has deployed three vessels that could ship aid to coastal communities isolated by the hurricane.

One of the towns in the hurricane’s projected path is San Juanico, a small fishing community on Baja’s Pacific coast. The town has only had full-time electricity for a few years, and still experiences frequent outages. There is concern that washed-out roads could block access to the closest medical facility, about 80 minutes away in Ciudad Constitución.

“Our people are concerned about this event,” said Gloriely Robles Meza, a manager at a small hotel. “We haven’t faced such a worrying situation in many years.”

Robles Meza said on Sunday that the Mexican army arrived in San Juanico to prepare a shelter and to provide support for possible emergencies. An electrical crew was also there to prepare for Polo’s arrival.

Also on Sunday, tropical storm Rachel formed well off Mexico’s south-west coast, the Miami-based US hurricane center said. It added that Rachel had maximum sustained winds of 40mph and was located about 300 miles (south of Acapulco, Mexico. No coastal watches or warnings were in effect.

rss_7_1790805688.title: Melbourne man’s mysterious disappearance on popular Peru hiking trail prompts widespread search
rss_7_1790805688.text:
Loved ones of a missing Australian trekker who was last seen nearly two weeks ago on a remote South American hiking trail are urging local authorities to help with the search.

A wide-scale sweep by a private rescue crew has so far failed to find any trace of 30-year-old Jordan Yap, who last made contact with friends and family on 14 September ahead of a planned 10-day solo trek along Peru’s Huayhuash mountain range, 400km north-east of Lima.

He was last seen near the beginning of his trek across the Cordillera Huayhuash circuit, which is regarded as a challenging, high-altitude trek through the remote Andes mountains.

Regarded as a very experienced hiker by friends and family, the Melbourne man failed to make contact on Wednesday, his estimated return date.

View image in fullscreen Family and friends are urging the Australian government to work with Peruvian officials and local authorities to mobilise further resources in and around the rugged region. Photograph: AAP/Supplied by Kevin Nguyen

He also failed to check back into the Krusty hostel in Huaraz, where his luggage remains stored, and missed a scheduled flight from Lima to Cusco on Thursday.

“It’s really uncharacteristic of him to not have communicated at any point in his journey if he had the chance to,” longtime friend Kevin Nguyen said.

“It is a very popular trek, where you might have 200 to 300 hikers and guides per week during the busy season, so it is very uncharacteristic that no one’s seen him since day one or day two.”

The avid trekker misplaced a satellite beacon he was travelling with days before he set off on the 120km hike, raising further concerns.

Local mountain rescue organisation Socorro Andino Peruano has been hired by Yap’s family to help with the search.

His loved ones are holding out hope the rescue group, which recently rescued a Canadian trekker from the same trail, will be able to find him safe.

“Time is of the essence … because ultimately, as much as we were saying he’s been missing since the 23rd, he’s had no contact with anyone since the 14th,” Nguyen said.

Rescue crews completed their biggest day of search operations so far on Saturday (Sunday morning AEST), scouring various trails on the circuit to no avail.

“I know Jordan likes to orienteer and navigate and he’s quite an adventurer himself, so I wouldn’t be surprised if he tried an alternative route,” Nguyen said.

Yap had been planning the trek for more than a year and had recently bought a GPS watch to allow for offline maps to guide him on the hike.

“He was telling everyone about how he was ready to go on a big hike like this, [he was] really excited,” Nguyen said.

He was last known to be wearing a white jacket, green sunshade sweater and grey pants.

The experienced trekker was believed to be carrying a 40-litre hiking bag, Durston dome tent and hiking poles.

Family and friends are urging the Australian government to work with Peruvian officials and local authorities to mobilise further resources in and around the rugged region.

The Australian embassy in Peru is helping his family.

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade has been contacted for comment.

rss_8_1790805688.title: US strikes on Ecuadorian fishing boats raise humanitarian concerns but Trump admin not wavering
rss_8_1790805688.text:
While the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, was being decorated in Quito by Ecuador’s president for “helping to promote peace in the region”, 10 Ecuadorian fishers whose boat had been blown up by US forces were adrift in the eastern Pacific.

View image in fullscreen Ecuador’s president, Daniel Noboa, right, presents the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, with Ecuador’s highest ranking National Order of Merit, the Grand Cross, at Carondelet palace in Quito, on 9 September. Photograph: Dolores Ochoa/AP

On 8 September, a day before Rubio arrived, a US patrol vessel intercepted the fishing boat Don Rufo in international waters near Ecuador.

“The gringos were all armed as if they were going to war,” said the boat’s captain, Mero Calderón, 50. “I tried to show them our catch to prove that we were there working, but they wouldn’t listen,” he added.

View image in fullscreen A US patrol vessel intercepting the fishing boat Don Rufo in international waters near Ecuador. Photograph: US Southern Command/X

“They brought two huge bombs aboard, took us to their ship, handcuffed and blindfolded us, and blew our boat to pieces,” said Calderón, who along with five other fishers, was handed over to local authorities.

But another 10 crew members were fishing farther out to sea in a smaller boat that was not equipped to make it back to shore. The Ecuadorian navy only rescued them on 10 September, when Rubio was already in Peru preparing to return to the US.

View image in fullscreen Ten crew members from the five skiffs belonging to the vessel Don Rufo, after they were located and taken aboard the BAE Atahualpa, following air-maritime search and reconnaissance operations conducted by the Ecuadorian navy. Photograph: Ecuadorian Navy

US Southern Command posted an edited 14-second video of the operation and said “intelligence confirmed” that the vessel was being used by a gang as a “floating refuelling station” for speedboats allegedly carrying drugs – which the fishers deny.

It was one of eight operations involving Ecuadorian boats in just more than two weeks – the latest on 16 September – to follow the same pattern. Unlike the nearly 70 US airstrikes in the Pacific and Caribbean that have killed 234 people since last year, crews were removed before the vessels were sunk.

View image in fullscreen A still from a video released by US forces intercepting a floating refuelling station supporting illicit at-sea drug trafficking operations in the eastern Pacific. Photograph: US Southern Command @Southcom

Also, rather than unilateral US attacks, the new wave of operations has the open support of Ecuador’s far-right president, Daniel Noboa, who is calling them “joint operations”.

Donald Trump has compared the drug trafficking operations to the campaign against the Islamic state. “Like ISIS, they should be killed, exiled or detained as enemy combatants without the possibility of release, which is what we’re doing,” Trump said on Tuesday.

Some analysts see the shift as an indication that the US’s military strategy against drug trafficking in Latin America has entered a new phase.

View image in fullscreen Marines and sailors with Maritime Raid Force, LCF-24, boarding the Ecuadorian fishing vessel Conquista 2 in the Pacific on 2 September. Photograph: US Marine Corps Forces, South

“Noboa has offered Ecuador as a ‘laboratory’ for the implementation of this new phase,” said Will Freeman, a fellow for Latin America studies at the Council on Foreign Relations.

Although Ecuador does not produce cocaine like neighbouring Colombia and Peru, over the past decade it has become a major trafficking hub because of its access to the Pacific, including the area where the attacks on boats have been taking place.

Noboa has responded with a controversial “iron-fist” approach to the gangs, issuing repeated states of emergency and expanding the role of the armed forces.

View image in fullscreen Relatives of the four minors apprehended by soldiers and found dead near a military base dance during a rally to demand justice a year after their apprehension in Guayaquil, Ecuador on 8 December 2025. Photograph: Marcos Pin/AFP/Getty Images

This crackdown however has done little to reduce violence, and instead has eroded human rights. The most notable example of human rights abuse came last year in the case of the “Guayaquil Four”, the forced disappearance of four Afro-Ecuadorian boys between the age of 11 and 15. All four boys were found dead, there bodies charred and dismembered.

Despite pushback from voters, Noboa signed an agreement with the White House authorising joint operations and granting US military personnel involved in counter-narcotics operations immunity from criminal prosecution. The operations have also extended to land, with US troops taking part in raids last Thursday.

“Noboa is interested in the optics of a very lethal crackdown and in making Ecuador a place where the Trump administration can refine those methods and show them off,” said Freeman, who has also reported on the boat attacks in Ecuador for the New Yorker magazine.

View image in fullscreen People look at the remains of a burned-out fishing boat in the port of Manta, Ecuador, on 6 June 2026. The Ecuadorian national police said at least 20 fishing boats had been damaged. Photograph: Ariel Ochoa/EPA

View image in fullscreen The Ecuadorean army shows drug trafficker Adolfo Macías, alias Fito, being guarded after his recapture in Manta, which is in the Manabi province. Photograph: Ecuadorean Army/AFP/Getty Images

Trump has pressured Latin American presidents to join an anti-drug cartel coalition he created called Shield of the Americas. With Peru and Colombia recently joining, the group now includes all but the few countries still governed by the left, such as Mexico and Brazil – where a far-right senator is a serious contender in October’s election.

So far, the coalition’s primary goal appears to have been increasing joint operations against alleged drug traffickers.

Adam Isacson, director for defence oversight at the Washington Office on Latin America, expects joint operations to expand across the region.

View image in fullscreen Fishermen work along the shore as local fishermen are increasingly being pursued by Ecuadorean gangs to move drugs and for their skills navigating the Pacific waters along Ecuador’s coast, in Manta, on 4 June. Photograph: Karen Toro/Reuters

Isacson stressed that though more people are being turned over to local authorities instead of killed, the US is “still doing the bad old stuff”. On 19 September, four people were killed in the Caribbean. As with the other airstrikes, the US has not disclosed their identities or any of the alleged evidence linking them to criminal activity.

During his trip to Ecuador, Rubio said the decision on what approach to take was “a strike-by-strike or operation-by-operation determination” that depended on the threat and location of the boat, but that the US would “still blow up ships if need be”.

Human rights organisations have described the airstrikes as extrajudicial killings, and a special rapporteur for the UN human rights council has concluded that there are “reasonable grounds to believe” that they constitute “crimes against humanity”.

Despite Trump’s claims, available data show they have had no impact on the volume of cocaine entering the country.

Journalists and human rights groups have managed to identify some of the victims, who in many cases were innocent or, when suspected of involvement in criminal activity, poor people at the bottom of trafficking networks.

View image in fullscreen Relatives wait for 32 crew members to be released under precautionary measures in Manta, Ecuador, on 8 September 2026. The 24 crew members of the Maria Candelaria and eight from the Conquista II face judicial proceedings on suspicion of illicit association and fuel trafficking after their vessels were intercepted and destroyed by US forces in the Pacific Ocean. Photograph: Ariel Ochoa/EPA

In Ecuador, the local NGO Permanent Committee for the Defence of Human Rights estimates that more than 220 fishers have been subjected to “violent boardings, arbitrary detentions, enforced disappearances, torture and the destruction of vessels” in this year’s US operations.

None of the fishers remains in custody and, while some are still facing prosecution, many have already been acquitted for lack of evidence.

“Fishers are losing their livelihoods when the US destroys the boats. Besides, if the US says the vessels were being used to refuel drug boats, why destroy the evidence?” said the committee’s lawyer, Fernando Bastías.

A US Southern Command spokesperson said it conducts operations “in compliance with US and international law” and that leaving boats “intact could permit their reuse by criminal networks”.

Although the US and Ecuador have celebrated the recent operations on social media, three cases from earlier this year remain unclaimed.

The first was on 20 January, when the fishing vessel Fiorella disappeared with eight crew members on board; days earlier, some of them had told relatives they were being monitored by drones and by a vessel on which they said they had seen a US flag.

Human rights organisations and journalists identified two more cases with similar patterns in late March, although the fishers survived. The Washington Post reported that the three cases were part of a covert CIA programme, and the agency declined to comment.

A US Southern Command spokesperson said it had no knowledge of, nor were its forces “involved in the incidents described in reports involving the Fiorella”.

View image in fullscreen Maria Mero and her mother, Maria Cueva, speak during an interview after Mero’s husband Gabriel Aladino Mero Delgado and brother Jefferson Ariel Mero Cueva disappeared from the boat Fiorella after a strike in June 2026. Photograph: Karen Toro/Reuters

View image in fullscreen Maria Cueva holding a picture of her son Jefferson Ariel Mero Cueva. Photograph: Karen Toro/Reuters

Both the husband and brother of María Mero, 43, were aboard the Fiorella: Gabriel Aladino Mero Delgado, 44, and Jefferson Ariel Mero Cueva, 25. “Where did they take them? Do they have them in the US, in a prison somewhere? We don’t want any trouble; we just want them to send them back to us,” she told the Guardian.

The families say they have spent months trying to get answers from the Ecuadorian government, so far without success.

“They were fishers, not criminals. Let the great president come here to my house and see whether I have luxuries, anything that would show I’m a drug trafficker. No, because all of us here are poor, and we just want our loved ones back,” added Mero.

rss_9_1790805689.title: Lula bans fixed-odds sports betting a week before Brazilian elections
rss_9_1790805689.text:
The Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has signed an order banning fixed-odds sports betting just over a week before the first round of the presidential election, in a move he said was designed to tackle the pervasive problem of families falling into debt.

The decision ends the operation, offering, intermediation and advertising of betting.

The provisional executive order comes into force immediately but will need congressional approval within 120 days to remain in effect. It prohibits new deposits into accounts and gives users of betting platforms until 5 October to withdraw their funds.

Lula’s government has also drafted a bill to establish criminal offences related to fixed-odds betting – the most common and dominant type of online sports betting – such as promoting them and using personal data to solicit punters.

“I made the decision to take a hard, drastic and necessary measure,” he told journalists in São Paulo. “It’s like cancer, you take out the tumour, or the tumour will kill us.”

Lula had also criticised the betting industry earlier this week at the UN general assembly, accusing it of “transforming addiction into profit” and of “destroying homes”.

Polls suggest a ban enjoys widespread support among Brazilians. Flávio Bolsonaro, Lula’s main rival in the coming election, accused the current leader of an “electoral measure”.

Brazil’s president has sharply criticised online betting at least since April, when he called for a ban. The public backlash against it grew during the Fifa World Cup when advertisements were ubiquitous and the number of people betting surged.

Betting and gambling are estimated to cost Brazilian society 38.8bn reais (£5.6bn) annually and increases suicide and depression, according to a 2025 study by the nonprofit Institute of Studies for Health Policies.

The country’s central bank estimated last year that Brazilians spend about 30bn reais on bets each month. That figure included spending by beneficiaries of the cash-transfer federal welfare programme Bolsa Familia (family grant), which was blocked from those platforms last year.

Lawmakers, including many from Flávio Bolsonaro’s Liberal party, struck down a Lula order for tax hikes on online betting and virtual casinos in October last year.

Gambling is illegal in Brazil, but the country opened the gates to online betting in 2018 during the presidency of Michel Temer. The phenomenon snowballed under the watch of the former president, Jair Bolsonaro, Flávio Bolsonaro’s father.

In December 2023, Lula signed a law to regulate and tax betting companies for the first time. Months later, his administration blocked more than 2,000 online betting websites that were designated as irregular, including some linked to criminal organisations such as the First Capital Command from São Paulo and the Red Command of Rio de Janeiro. It was part of a national push to regulate the sector.

Lula and members of his administration have spoken about banning online betting as necessary to close a drain to the country’s economy and to tackle a public health issue, as many Brazilians are addicted and in financial difficulties due to spending their money on these platforms.

Business analysts say that revenues for sports betting, one of the betting models banned on Friday, are estimated at more than $4bn (£3bn) per year in Brazil, one of the biggest markets in the world.

Before Friday’s move, Brazil’s main football clubs sounded the alarm after betting companies reportedly warned that their sponsorships would end immediately if the government banned betting.

They said the move could lead to the end of Brazilian football, a claim mocked by some social media users in the football-mad country.
